In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of diffusion tensor imaging to study the microstructure of the brain, with an emphasis on the application of these techniques to the study of brain tumors.
the development of new methods to characterize and quantify the directional properties of diffusion in the human brain using the color‐coded diffusion‐tensor‐derived map.
the development of new methods for the quantitative analysis of DTI data in order to improve the diagnostic specificity of DTI in the characterization of brain tumors.

the directionally encoded color maps provide the most complete picture of diffusion tensor properties, but the directional statistics provide a means for quantitatively assessing the distribution of tensor properties in a region of interest.
the use of directional statistical methods in DTI is still a relatively unexplored area, and the results of the present study suggest that it may be a fruitful one for future research.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the diffusion direction is the most reliable and robust DTI feature for discriminating tumor from normal brain, and that the color map is a powerful tool for its visualization.
the principal diffusional direction in peritumoral fiber tracts tends to deviate from that in the normal brain.
the principal diffusion direction in peritumoral fiber tracts is not random.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the principal diffusion direction (PDD) is a powerful tool in the analysis of peritumoral fiber tracts.
the principal diffusion direction (PDD) in peritumoral fiber tracts may be a useful biomarker for the presence of neoplasm in the brain.
the principal diffusion direction (PDD) is a useful and informative measure of the diffusion properties of brain tissues.
